options.text: right to vote in an election
right to be appointed a minister
duty of INEC to print ballot papers
power of a court to cancel a result

questions.explanation: Suffrage, also called the franchise, is the legal right to vote. Nigeria practises universal adult suffrage: a citizen who is 18, registered and not legally disqualified may vote. The other options are powers or rights, but they are not suffrage.

distractorRationale.b: Eligibility for ministerial office is a separate constitutional question, not the franchise
distractorRationale.c: Printing materials is an administrative duty of the electoral body
distractorRationale.d: Cancelling a result is a judicial function of election tribunals and appellate courts

questions.stem: Under the simple-majority (first-past-the-post) system, a candidate is elected when he or she

options.text: obtains more votes than any other candidate, even if that is less than half of the votes cast
obtains two-thirds of the votes in two-thirds of the states
is assigned a share of seats equal to the party's percentage of the national vote
is the only candidate remaining after all others have been eliminated in successive rounds

questions.explanation: Plurality, not an absolute majority, is enough. If A has 40 per cent, B 35 per cent and C 25 per cent, A wins the seat. That is the rule used for Nigeria's Senate, House of Representatives and State Houses of Assembly. It is simple, but a candidate can win without most voters having chosen him or her.

distractorRationale.b: A territorial two-thirds-and-a-quarter test belongs to Nigeria's presidential election, not to FPTP
distractorRationale.c: Sharing seats by percentage is proportional representation
distractorRationale.d: Successive elimination describes some preferential or run-off systems, not simple majority

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC)?

options.text: Appointing ministers of the Federal Government
Registering political parties and conducting general elections
Interpreting the Constitution in election disputes as a final court
Preparing the national budget

questions.explanation: The Third Schedule to the 1999 Constitution charges INEC with organising elections, compiling the voters' register, registering and monitoring parties, delimiting constituencies, conducting voter education and declaring results. Appointment of ministers, final constitutional interpretation and the budget belong to other organs.

distractorRationale.a: Ministers are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate
distractorRationale.c: Election petitions are heard by tribunals and the regular courts, with the Supreme Court at the apex for presidential disputes
distractorRationale.d: The budget is prepared by the executive and passed by the National Assembly

sources.title: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, Third Schedule Part I F

questions.stem: A distinctive feature of Nigeria's presidential electoral system under section 134 of the 1999 Constitution is that the winner must

options.text: win a simple majority in the Federal Capital Territory only
obtain the highest number of votes and not less than one-quarter of the votes in at least two-thirds of the states and the FCT
be returned unopposed in at least 24 states
secure a proportion of National Assembly seats equal to his or her share of the popular vote

questions.explanation: Section 134 combines a plurality of the national vote with a geographical-spread test: at least 25 per cent in each of two-thirds of all the states and the FCT. If that double requirement is not met, a second ballot is held. The rule is designed to prevent a purely regional candidate from becoming President of a federation.

distractorRationale.a: Winning the FCT alone would not satisfy the nationwide spread test
distractorRationale.c: Unopposed returns in 24 states are not a constitutional requirement
distractorRationale.d: Linking seats to vote share is proportional representation, which Nigeria does not use for the presidency

sources.title: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, section 134

questions.stem: Which of the following is a form of electoral malpractice?

options.text: Displaying the voters' register for public claims and objections
Ballot-box snatching and vote buying
Issuing a Permanent Voter's Card to a registered adult citizen
Collating results at a designated centre in the presence of party agents

questions.explanation: Snatching a ballot box removes votes already cast; vote buying substitutes money for free choice. Both distort the election. Displaying the register, issuing cards to qualified adults, and open collation are lawful safeguards, not malpractices.

distractorRationale.a: Public display of the register is a legal step that allows names to be corrected
distractorRationale.c: Issuing a card to a qualified registered voter is INEC's duty
distractorRationale.d: Open collation with agents present is a transparency measure

questions.stem: Nigeria uses proportional representation to elect members of the National Assembly.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. The 109 senators and 360 representatives are elected by simple majority in single-member constituencies — first-past-the-post. Proportional representation, which shares seats according to each party's share of the vote, is not the system used for Nigeria's federal legislature.

distractorRationale.a: Students sometimes confuse the large number of parties with proportional seating; the counting rule remains plurality in each constituency
